meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All disease begins in the gut'?
meta.ogDescription: No surviving Hippocratic text contains it. Here's what the corpus actually says about a single cause of all disease — and it isn't the gut.

answer.label: Not Hippocrates — an unsourced modern saying
answer.authorDates: Originator unidentified · no ancient source documented
answer.sourceLine: The line is pinned on Hippocrates by wellness sites, supplement brands and peer-reviewed journals alike, but it appears in no surviving Hippocratic text. A 2026 review in the Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition puts it plainly: “the precise phrase ‘all disease begins in the gut’ does not appear in the extant Hippocratic writings.” No ancient source has ever been produced, and no modern coiner has been identified.

source.heading: What the Hippocratic writings actually say

docMeta.dd: Not present in the extant Hippocratic writings
The Genuine Works of Hippocrates, trans. Francis Adams (New York: William Wood, 1886)

source.excerpt: The manner of all diseases is the same, but they differ in place… For there is but one form (ἰδίη) of all disease, and the cause is the same. What that is I will attempt to explain in the following discourse. The bodies of men and of other animals are nourished by three kinds of aliment, namely, food, drink, and airs; and those winds in the body are called spirits, which are named airs out of it.
trail: Wikiquote’s Hippocrates page ↗ does not carry this line anywhere — not among the sourced quotations, not even among the disputed ones, which do cover “Let food be thy medicine” with the note that it “does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus.”

The journal Brain put the slogan in a 2018 headline as a question — “was Hippocrates right?” — and the piece opened by hedging the attribution: Hippocrates “apparently claimed” it. Louisa Lyon, Brain 141(3): e20 ↗.

The plainest published verdict is Yukio Nagasaki’s 2026 review in the Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition: the precise phrase “does not appear in the extant Hippocratic writings” ↗, though it is commonly attributed to him.

Searching Francis Adams’s 1886 translation turns up no sentence of this kind — but it does turn up the corpus’s own one-cause claim, in the treatise Adams calls On Airs ↗, where the single cause of all disease is air.
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote’s source — there isn’t one. It is the closest the Hippocratic collection comes to declaring a single cause for all disease, and the cause it names is air, not the gut. Adams adds that this treatise, accepted by the ancient authorities, was “rejected by the modern,” and that Littré “refuses it a place in his list of genuine works.”

sourceLink.text: The Genuine Works of Hippocrates, trans. Francis Adams (1886), on Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: Two separate questions, and only one has an answer. The ancient Greek is long out of copyright, and Francis Adams’s translation, first published in 1886, is public domain in the United States. But this sentence is in neither — it has no identified author, work or date of first publication, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for the wording itself.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: The man it gets pinned on
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos, the ‘father of medicine’
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos was a Greek physician of the fifth and fourth centuries BC, remembered for treating illness as a natural process with natural causes rather than a punishment from the gods. The roughly sixty works of the Hippocratic Corpus have travelled under his name since antiquity, yet none of them is proven to be his own writing. That gap — a towering name attached to texts nobody can pin to him — is exactly what makes him one of the most reliable magnets for invented quotations on the internet.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source. Attribution examined in Louisa Lyon, “‘All disease begins in the gut’: was Hippocrates right?” Brain 141, no. 3 (2018): e20; and Yukio Nagasaki, “Controlling systemic disease from the gut: intestinal ROS as an upstream driver of systemic inflammation,” Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition 78, no. 3 (2026): 169–180, which states the phrase does not appear in the extant Hippocratic writings. Corpus text consulted: Hippocrates, The Genuine Works of Hippocrates, trans. Francis Adams (New York: William Wood, 1886).

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on him
misattribution.intro: This is not a mangled quotation. There is no original to mangle — the sentence has no documented source in any language, ancient or modern, and Hippocrates’s name simply travels with it.

items.why: A 2026 review in the Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition states it directly: “Although the precise phrase ‘all disease begins in the gut’ does not appear in the extant Hippocratic writings, it is commonly attributed to Hippocrates.” Read the passage ↗. Wikiquote’s Hippocrates page ↗ does not carry the line anywhere, sourced or disputed.

“All diseases begin in the gut” and “All disease starts in the gut” circulate just as widely, and fare no better. A 2021 review in Rheumatology Advances in Practice writes that Hippocrates “supposedly declared” it ↗; a 2024 review in Frontiers in Medicine says it is “often attributed to Hippocrates circa 400 BC” ↗. Neither names a text.

He collects these. Wikipedia notes that “Let food be your medicine, and medicine be your food” and “Walking is man’s best medicine” are both likely misquotations of unknown origin ↗; McGill’s Joe Schwarcz found “no record of such a statement in the ‘Hippocratic Corpus’” ↗ for the food line, and Wikiquote credits a 2013 paper by Diana Cardenas with documenting it as a misquotation ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No surviving Hippocratic text contains the sentence. The nearest the collection comes to claiming one cause for every disease is in the treatise Adams titles On Airs, where the cause named is air — and Adams records that even that treatise, accepted in antiquity, was “rejected by the modern” critics ↗, with Littré refusing it a place among the genuine works.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: The line took off with the microbiome. As gut bacteria became the most exciting story in medicine, a six-word slogan from the “father of medicine” made a young field sound 2,400 years old. It now opens papers in Brain, Frontiers in Medicine and Rheumatology Advances in Practice — and every one of them quietly hedges. ‘Apparently claimed’ ↗. ‘Supposedly declared’ ↗. ‘Often attributed’ ↗. Nobody cites a page.

It is a strange fit even on its own terms. Hippocratic medicine cared enormously about diet, digestion and regimen, but it explained illness through the humours, not the intestine. And the one place in the collection that claims a single cause for every disease names air — not the gut. The slogan is a modern idea wearing ancient clothes.
context.detailsSummary: Two things worth knowing before you quote it
detailsBody: “Hippocrates said” is a shakier phrase than it sounds, even for genuine passages. The Hippocratic Corpus ↗ is a collection of around sixty early Greek medical works, and the scholarly summary is blunt: “Of the texts in the corpus, none is proven to be by Hippocrates himself.” So even a line that genuinely is in the corpus is Hippocratic only by tradition.

Where the sentiment does live in its own voice is the nature-cure tradition. A 2019 history of naturopathy in Integrative Medicine: A Clinician’s Journal states the doctrine flatly — “all disease begins in the gut and all healing must also begin there” ↗ — and traces it not to Hippocrates but to Priessnitz, Kneipp, Lindlahr and Lust. That tells you where the idea is at home. It is not evidence of who coined the sentence, and the coiner remains unidentified.
context.pull: Every journal that quotes it hedges. None of them cites a text.

sourcesVerified.claim: Louisa Lyon's 2018 Brain article opens: "Hippocrates apparently claimed that 'All disease begins in the gut'" — hedging the attribution rather than confirming it.
Bibliographic record for the Brain article: Louisa Lyon, "'All disease begins in the gut': was Hippocrates right?", Brain, vol. 141, issue 3, pages e20-e20, published 12 February 2018.

Yukio Nagasaki, "Controlling systemic disease from the gut", Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition 78(3):169-180 (2026), states: "Although the precise phrase 'all disease begins in the gut' does not appear in the extant Hippocratic writings, it is commonly attributed to Hippocrates, reflecting the long-standing recognition of the importance of the gut in systemic health."
Guarner et al., Frontiers in Medicine (2024), write: "The quotation 'all disease begins in the gut' is often attributed to Hippocrates circa 400 BC."
The 2021 Rheumatology Advances in Practice review writes: "More than 2000 years ago, Hippocrates supposedly declared that 'all disease begins in the gut'".

Wikiquote's Hippocrates page does not list "All disease begins in the gut" anywhere; its disputed list does include "Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food" with the note that it "is often attributed to Hippocrates but does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus", crediting Diana Cardenas's 2013 publication for documenting the misquotation.

Wikipedia gives Hippocrates's dates as c. 460 - c. 370 BC and states: "Two popular but likely misquoted attributions to Hippocrates are 'Let food be your medicine, and medicine be your food' and 'Walking is man's best medicine.' Both appear to be misquotations, and their exact origins remain unknown." It does not list "all disease begins in the gut".

Wikipedia's Hippocratic Corpus article describes it as "a collection of around 60 early Ancient Greek medical works" and states: "Of the texts in the corpus, none is proven to be by Hippocrates himself."

Project Gutenberg ebook #72583 is 'The genuine works of Hippocrates, Vol. 1 (of 2)', translated by Francis Adams, originally published New York: William Wood, 1886. Its text contains no occurrence of 'in the gut' or 'disease begins'; under the heading 'XXIII. Peri physon — On Airs' it renders: 'For there is but one form of all disease, and the cause is the same... The bodies of men and of other animals are nourished by three kinds of aliment, namely, food, drink, and airs', and notes the treatise is 'generally admitted by the ancient authorities, but rejected by the modern', with Littre refusing 'it a place in his list of genuine works'.

Joe Schwarcz of McGill's Office for Science and Society writes of 'let food be thy medicine': "The problem here is that there is no record of such a statement in the 'Hippocratic Corpus.'" The article does not mention 'all disease begins in the gut'.

A 2019 naturopathy history in Integrative Medicine: A Clinician's Journal states in its own voice: "In regards to the vital processes of the body, all disease begins in the gut and all healing must also begin there", placing it in the tradition of Priessnitz, Kneipp, Lindlahr and Lust, with no mention of Hippocrates.
